lesson.title: Electrons on Rails: The Bohr Model of the Atom
lesson.summary: The Bohr model placed electrons in fixed, quantized circular orbits around the nucleus and explained why atoms absorb and emit light only at specific wavelengths, setting the stage for the modern quantum picture of the atom.
lesson.body:
By the early 1900s, Rutherford's gold foil experiment had established that atoms have a tiny, dense, positively charged nucleus with negatively charged electrons somewhere around it, part of the broader story of atomic theory's historical development. But Rutherford's model had a serious flaw: classical physics predicted that an orbiting electron should continuously radiate energy and spiral into the nucleus within a fraction of a second, meaning atoms should not be stable at all. In 1913, the Danish physicist Niels Bohr proposed a bold fix specifically for the hydrogen atom, combining Rutherford's nuclear structure with the new idea that energy could be quantized, meaning restricted to specific allowed values rather than any value at all.

Bohr's model proposed that electrons travel around the nucleus only in certain fixed, circular orbits, each corresponding to a specific, quantized energy level labeled by a whole number n, now called the principal quantum number. While in one of these allowed orbits, an electron does not radiate energy and the atom is stable, directly solving Rutherford's stability problem. An electron can move from one orbit to another only by absorbing or emitting a photon whose energy exactly equals the difference in energy between the two orbits. This explained why atoms absorb and emit light only at specific wavelengths rather than a continuous range, producing the sharp line spectra that had puzzled physicists for decades.

The model comes with a specific energy formula for the hydrogen atom: E_n = -2.18 x 10^-18 J / n^2, where n is the orbit number. As a worked example, consider an electron falling from the n=3 orbit to the n=2 orbit, a transition that produces one of the visible lines in hydrogen's spectrum. The energy of the n=3 level is E_3 = -2.18 x 10^-18 / 9 = -2.42 x 10^-19 J, and the energy of the n=2 level is E_2 = -2.18 x 10^-18 / 4 = -5.45 x 10^-19 J. The energy released as the electron drops is the difference, about 3.03 x 10^-19 J, emitted as a single photon. Using E = hc/λ with Planck's constant h = 6.626 x 10^-34 J s and the speed of light c = 3.00 x 10^8 m/s, this photon's wavelength works out to about 656 nm, which is the well known red line in hydrogen's visible emission spectrum, part of what is called the Balmer series. The close match between Bohr's calculated value and the experimentally observed red line was strong evidence in favor of the model when it was first proposed.

Despite this early success, the Bohr model has real limits. It works remarkably well for hydrogen and other single electron systems, but it fails to correctly predict the spectra of atoms with more than one electron, because it does not account for the way electrons interact with and repel one another. It also treats electrons as tiny particles moving in precise, well defined circular paths, an idea that later turned out to conflict with the wave-like behavior electrons actually display.

These shortcomings did not erase Bohr's contribution; they set the direction for the next major advance. The core idea that electron energy is quantized into discrete levels survived and remains true, but the picture of electrons as particles on fixed circular orbits was replaced by a more complete description, the quantum mechanical model, which treats electron position as a matter of probability rather than a definite path.
